topic: How to Check a Flight Reservation PNR Yourself Before You Submit It
metaTitle: How to Check a Flight Reservation PNR Before You Send It
metaDescription: Check your flight reservation PNR yourself before you submit it. How the GDS lookup works, why many airline sites show nothing, and how to spot a fake PDF.
excerpt: A flight reservation is only as good as the record behind it, and you can check that record in about two minutes. This guide walks through the GDS lookup, explains why many airline websites will show you nothing, and lists the warning signs of a document that was never a real booking.
quickAnswer: Check it in the GDS, not on the airline's website. A real flight reservation carries a six-character alphanumeric record locator that returns your name, route and dates when you enter it into the Amadeus, Sabre or Travelport traveller lookup. Airline Manage Booking pages often show nothing for an unpaid hold, so a blank result there proves nothing either way.
content:
You can check it yourself in about two minutes, and you should never submit a document you have not looked up. The reliable test is a GDS lookup: type the six-character booking reference into the traveller lookup run by whichever system holds the record, Amadeus, Sabre or Travelport, and see whether a live reservation comes back with your name, route and dates on it. The airline's own Manage Booking page is a bonus, not the test.

What is a PNR, and is it the same as my booking reference?

A PNR is the record itself. The European Commission describes PNR data as information provided by passengers and held in air carriers' reservation and departure control systems for their own commercial purposes. Every journey that gets booked creates one.

The booking reference, sometimes called the record locator, is the short code that points at that record. People use "PNR" to mean both. In practice, when a visa centre or a check-in agent asks for your PNR, they want the code.

Here is the part that matters for anyone nervous about a reservation: a PNR exists before anyone pays a fare. IATA's own description of the data says a PNR can include as little as a name, an itinerary and a ticket indicator. The ticket indicator is a separate field. A booking with no ticket issued against it is still a booking, and it still sits in the system under a real code.

That is the whole basis of a held reservation. It is not a picture of a ticket. It is a genuine seat hold with the fare left unpaid, which is why it can expire and why we sell it by how long it stays live.

What should you check, at a glance?

ItemWhat to expect
What a PNR isA record created and held in an airline or agency reservation system for each journey booked (European Commission)
What it can containAs little as a name, an itinerary and a ticket indicator (IATA)
Booking reference formatSix characters, letters and numbers, in the systems you will meet. No single global standard fixes the format
Where the check worksThe Amadeus, Sabre or Travelport traveller lookup for the system holding the record
Airline Manage BookingSome carriers display an unpaid hold. Many never do
Our reservation validity2 days (AED 49), 7 days (AED 69), 14 days (AED 79), per traveller
Delivery10 to 15 minutes after payment, around the clock

What do you need in front of you before you start?

  • The PDF itself, opened on a laptop rather than a phone, so you can read the small print
  • The six-character booking reference, copied exactly, including any zeros or ones that look like letters
  • Your passport, open at the photo page
  • The surname as the airline spells it, which is the surname on your passport and nothing else
  • The visa centre's document checklist, if you are building an application file
  • The date of your appointment or your flight, so you can confirm the reservation is still live on that day

How do you check the PNR step by step?

Work through it in this order. Each step is quick, and the first one does most of the work.

One. Find the booking reference on the document. It is usually labelled booking reference, reservation code, record locator or PNR, near the top. Six characters, mixed letters and numbers.

Two. Identify which system the reservation sits in. A well-formatted flight itinerary says so, or the layout gives it away. If you cannot tell, try each of the three traveller lookups in turn.

Three. Open the traveller lookup for that system. Amadeus, Sabre and Travelport each run a public page where a passenger can pull up their own trip. You enter the reference and the surname.

Four. Enter the reference and the surname exactly as printed. Surname only, not the full name. If it fails, try the surname without spaces or hyphens, since the systems store it flattened.

Five. Read what comes back. You want your name, the flight numbers, the airports, the dates and the times, and they should match the PDF line for line. If the lookup returns a record, the reservation is real.

Six. Now try the airline's Manage Booking page with the same reference and surname. Treat whatever happens there as extra information, not as the verdict.

Seven. Check the expiry against your appointment date. A reservation that lapses two days before your interview is no use, however real it was on the day it was issued.

Why does the airline website say the booking cannot be found?

Because a lot of airline websites only look at tickets, not at holds. Their Manage Booking tool is built for passengers who have paid and want a seat or a bag, so it queries ticketed records and returns nothing for anything else.

Some carriers do show an unpaid hold, often with a payment deadline attached. Others show nothing at all until money changes hands, and a few use a booking reference on their own site that differs from the one in the GDS record, because a code can be reissued when the booking moves between systems.

So a blank screen on the airline's site does not tell you the reservation is fake. It also does not tell you it is real. That is exactly why we point people at the GDS lookup and say plainly that many airline sites will show them nothing. Anyone promising you that every airline website will display an unpaid hold is selling you a claim they cannot keep.

One more thing worth knowing. UK government guidance describes PNR data as information collected by airlines in the normal course of business to complete and process a booking. It is commercial data held for the carrier's own purposes, not a public register. Nobody outside the trade gets a universal search box.

What does a valid flight reservation actually look like?

It reads like something a machine produced, because it was. Expect the airline's two-letter code and flight number on each segment, three-letter airport codes, local departure and arrival times, the travel class, the aircraft or operating carrier where relevant, and the passenger name in surname-first format with a title appended.

Expect a status against each segment too. Reservation systems carry a status code for every leg, and a held booking shows as confirmed on the segment while the fare sits unpaid. The document should also carry an issue date and, on a time-limited hold, some indication of when it lapses.

Names are where real documents most often go wrong, and it is not the supplier's fault. The name on the reservation has to match the machine-readable line of your passport. If your passport shows a single name with no surname field, or your given names run to four words, say so when you order rather than correcting it afterwards.

Our itinerary format is the standard airline layout for exactly this reason. A document that looks like the one the airline would have emailed you raises fewer questions than a prettier one that does not.

How do you spot a PDF that was never a real booking?

Start with the lookup. If no system returns a record for the reference, nothing else on the page matters. Beyond that, these are the tells.

  • No booking reference at all, or one that is four characters, eight characters, or a long string with dashes. Real record locators are short and six characters in the systems you will encounter.
  • A reference that is all letters in a neat word, or one that repeats across two different documents for two different people.
  • Flight numbers that do not exist on that route. Look the flight number up on the airline's own timetable and see whether it flies where the PDF says it flies, on that day of the week.
  • Impossible times. A three-hour hop from Dubai to London, or an arrival before departure once you account for the time difference, means someone typed the document rather than pulled it.
  • A ticket number printed on a document that was never paid for. A held reservation has no ticket number. A 13-digit ticket number on an unpaid hold is either an error or an invention.
  • The word "ticket" used where "reservation" belongs. A hold is a reservation. A document that calls itself a paid ticket is making a claim the record does not support.
  • Editable text in an image-only file, or fonts that change mid-line, or a logo pasted at the wrong aspect ratio. Airline systems do not produce that.
  • No issue date and no expiry. Every genuine hold has a life span.

The honest summary is that presentation proves nothing and the lookup proves everything. Somebody with an hour and a PDF editor can produce a page that looks better than a real one. They cannot put a record into Amadeus.

What gets a reservation rejected, and how do you avoid it?

Expiry is the most common failure, and it is entirely avoidable. People buy a two-day reservation a fortnight before an appointment, then submit a document that lapsed before the officer opened the file. Match the validity to when the file will actually be read, not to when you paid.

Name mismatches come second. A middle name included on the reservation but absent from the passport, or a surname and given name swapped, gives a reviewer a reason to send the file back. Check it the moment the PDF arrives, while a free correction is easy.

Third is inconsistency across the file. If your reservation lands in Milan on the 12th and your hotel booking starts in Rome on the 10th, the file argues with itself. Officers read the documents together, not one at a time.

Fourth is the wrong expectation. A reservation is evidence of a travel arrangement. The European Commission notes that the EU visa code sets out the procedures and conditions for issuing short-stay visas, and Article 14 of that code is the provision on supporting documents. It asks for evidence of your arrangements, not proof that you have bought a fare. No reservation decides your application on its own, and any service telling you otherwise is overselling. Refusals turn on funds, ties and whether the story holds together.

Fifth, and specific to airlines rather than consulates, is the gate. Where a carrier insists on a paid onward ticket before it will board you, a hold is not what they are asking for. That is rarer than the forums suggest, but it happens, and you should know the difference before you are standing at the desk.

What does a verifiable reservation cost?

You are buying time, not distance. The tier sets how long the reservation stays live in the system. One way and return cost the same, and the price is per traveller.

ValidityPriceSuits
2 daysAED 49An appointment this week, or a check-in desk tomorrow
7 daysAED 69A visa file that will sit in a queue for a few days
14 daysAED 79A longer processing window, or a date you may need to move

There are no embassy or visa centre fees in that table because this is our fee only. Whatever the consulate charges is separate and goes to them.

If your appointment moves, we reissue with the new dates at no charge. And the document arrives 10 to 15 minutes after payment, at any hour, so you can run the lookup yourself before you go anywhere near a counter.

Want a reservation you can look up yourself?

We issue a genuine seat hold under a live PNR, in standard airline format, so the record locator returns a real booking when you check it in Amadeus, Sabre or Travelport. Book a flight itinerary from AED 49 and it reaches your inbox in 10 to 15 minutes, any hour of the day.

faqs.question: Is a PNR the same thing as a booking reference?
faqs.answer: Not quite. The PNR is the record held in the reservation system, and the booking reference or record locator is the short code that points at it. In everyday use the two words are swapped freely, and when someone asks for your PNR they want the code.

faqs.question: Can a PNR exist if nobody has paid for the flight?
faqs.answer: Yes. IATA describes a PNR as potentially containing as little as a name, an itinerary and a ticket indicator, and the ticket indicator is a separate field. A booking with no ticket issued against it is still a live record with a real reference.

faqs.question: Why does the airline site say my booking cannot be found?
faqs.answer: Because many Manage Booking tools only query ticketed records. An unpaid hold returns nothing on those sites, and some carriers use a different reference on their own site. The GDS traveller lookup is the check that actually settles it.

faqs.question: How long should a reservation stay valid for a visa file?
faqs.answer: Match the validity to when the file will be read, not when you pay. A two-day reservation at AED 49 suits an appointment this week. A file sitting in a queue is safer on the seven-day tier at AED 69 or the 14-day tier at AED 79.

faqs.question: What is the quickest sign a PDF was never a real booking?
faqs.answer: No record comes back from any of the three systems when you enter the reference. After that, look for a reference that is not six characters, a flight number that does not fly that route, or a ticket number printed on a document nobody paid for.
